D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b000_.text: This little skillet is sizzling one egg, honey, and listen to it. That sound is how my mornings came back. One egg, one small pan, one cold October morning in Iowa. Harold ate two eggs every morning for 51 years. After he was gone, I stopped eating breakfast. That was a mistake. The breakfast that brought me back to this table is number 10. 20 old farm breakfasts are coming, and every one is made for one. You'd think cooking for one means cooking less. I'm 81, widowed nine years in Iowa. For 60 years, I cooked for 100 people in the Zion United Methodist Church basement. Now I cook for one. So here are 20 old farm breakfasts, each for one, in one pan, for pennies. Wait for number eight, my mother's hard year's breakfast. Wait for number 20, where the end of the loaf goes. First the plainest one, oatmeal in my smallest pot.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b001_.text: number one and it's the plainest one. Do you still tear open an instant packet before the sun is up? Old-fashioned oats are the ones to use and I wrote it plain on page 53. Half a cup of oats, one cup of water or milk and a pinch of salt go in my smallest pot. Bring the liquid and salt to a boil then stir the oats in. Turn the heat to low and cook five minutes stirring now and then. Take Take it off the heat, put the lid on, and let it sit two minutes while it thickens. When I lift that lid, steam rises over one warm bowl on a cold October morning. The pinch of salt is what makes oatmeal taste like something. Don't skip it. Gluey oatmeal means it boiled too hard, honey. So on Sunday night, make five of these at once. Number two, five jars of overnight oats. Page 54. 10 minutes on Sunday night and five mornings are done.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b002_.text: Half a cup of oats, half a cup of milk, and a spoon of yogurt go in each jar. Penny's a jar. Add a shake of cinnamon and a little honey. Put the lid on and shake hard. Into the fridge they go. Good for five days. Frozen blueberries go in straight from the bag on Sunday. By Wednesday, they've made their own syrup. Wednesday, I reach to the back of the fridge, and there's the syrup. Purple streaks down the glass. Breakfast is already made, honey. Every one of these is one page of my little book, Supper for One. Next to each one, I wrote what it cost me at my grocery store this fall. You'll find the link below in the description, honey. Wondering where all these eggs and oats come from? My grocery video shows you, so go on and watch it. Stocking up, honey? My grocery video on this channel is called I'm 81 and only buy groceries twice a month, my haul for one.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b003_.text: It shows you where these eggs come from. Harold's two eggs and that little pan are still coming at number 10. Next, one batter for four mornings. Number three, and this is the box of pancake mix in your cupboard. A whole box makes 40 pancakes, honey. Far too many for one person. My batter makes 12 small ones, three a morning, all from one bowl. Leave the lumps in there. Stirring it smooth makes them tough as shoe leather. Pour a quarter cup at a time onto a lightly buttered skillet on medium. If the first one comes out pale, that's alright because the first one is always the cook's. Eat three, then freeze the rest flat with paper between them. Two rounds in the toaster on low and breakfast is on the table. It's all on page 55. And wait until you see what the end of the loaf nobody wants turns into. number four French toast from the heel of the bread page 56

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b004_.text: Most homes put the heel of the loaf in the bin, and nobody wants it. I wrote it plain in my book, Dry Bread Soaks Up More Egg, so I leave the heels out on the counter the night before, because stale bread holds the egg without falling apart. Next morning, one egg, a quarter cup of milk, a pinch of cinnamon, and a drop of vanilla, beaten in a pie plate. Soak each slice 30 seconds a side, then into a buttered skillet on medium. two to three minutes aside until golden. Two heels on one plate, syrup pooling in the corners, and it costs pennies a plate. Danny, come out from behind that camera, honey, and look at that plate. Danny's filming this, and he's already eyeing that plate, the heel nobody wanted, and he eats every bite. He doesn't look up from that plate, honey. Biscuits and gravy is next, honey, cut down to one small plate.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b005_.text: Number five is biscuits and gravy for one on page 57. Most homes bake the whole tube and a tube of biscuits for one person goes stale before the week is out. I brown a quarter pound of bulk pork sausage in one small skillet, breaking it up until no pink is left. Sprinkle in one tablespoon of flour and stir one minute. Pour in three quarters cup of milk, a little at a time, stirring, and cook until thick, about three minutes. Lots of black pepper, honey. Sausage must be cooked through, 160 degrees, with no pink. split two biscuits spoon the gravy over and there's your plate at a table set for one the rest of the tube goes in a bag raw in pairs bake them straight from frozen three or four minutes longer and the next breakfast is already waiting in your freezer number six a breakfast burrito for the freezer page 58

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b006_.text: Most mornings, somebody stands at the stove with one egg in a sticky pan. I make six on Sunday instead. Eggs, hash browns and sausage, rolled into tortillas. I wrote it plain in my book. Let the filling cool before you roll, or hot filling steams the tortilla and it goes soggy in the freezer. Each one gets a paper towel, then foil. Come morning, foil off, towel on, one minute, turn it, then 45 seconds more. Heat it to 165 degrees in the middle. Next is my mother's cinnamon toast, the cheapest one so far. Number seven is cinnamon toast the way mother made it, page 59. Most homes grab something and eat it standing up. two slices, butter all the way to the crust, two teaspoons of sugar with half a teaspoon of cinnamon, sprinkled thick and even, under the broiler until the sugar bubbles.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b007_.text: I wrote it plain in my book. It goes from bubbling to burnt in 30 seconds, so don't walk away. Keep that cinnamon sugar in an old salt shaker by the toaster, and it's ready every morning. About a quarter a plate and five minutes start to finish. Mother's kitchen, honey. Some mornings I'm a little girl watching her shake the sugar over the bread. Every time I make it, I'm standing in my mother's kitchen again. She had another one that started with almost nothing, a pot of cornmeal. Number eight, fried cornmeal mush, page 60. Most homes grab something quick and never think about what it costs. One cup of cornmeal makes a loaf pan that lasts eight mornings, honey, so a plate costs next to nothing. Cook it on Sunday, chill it overnight, and in the morning cut two slices half an inch thick. Fry them in butter, five minutes a side, until they're crisp.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b008_.text: If they splatter, the slices are wet. I wrote it plain in my book. Pat them dry first. A little flour on the slices makes the crust even crisper. Lay them golden on the plate with a spoon of syrup. Let me tell you about the hard years, when she made it. In the hard years, a pot of cornmeal was what we had, and Mother made it taste like plenty. Honey, that's the secret. Next, the little skillet heats up for the first egg of the list. Hash browns with one egg on top. Number nine, hash browns and one egg, page 62. Most folks stir them all morning. One cup of frozen hash browns and one tablespoon of oil go into an eight-inch skillet on medium-high. Once it shimmers, I spread them thin, press them down, and salt them. Then I leave them alone for five minutes. Stirring makes them mushy, honey, so I wrote it plain in my book. Turn them, cook four minutes more and push them aside.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b009_.text: The egg goes in the empty spot until the white is set, then slides on top. Lace edges, one egg, pennies on the plate. Before the two eggs that matter most, let me tell you about my book. Look in the cabinet by your stove, honey, at the pen you never use. Every breakfast here is in my little book, Supper for One. Point your phone at the little square on the screen, and it takes you straight to the book. Harold ate two eggs every morning, and the breakfast that brought me back to the table is next. Number 10. Listen to this. That little hiss when butter foams in a small pan is one of the coziest sounds on a cold October morning. Most homes grab the big skillet, pour in two eggs, and watch them spread out thin and turn to rubber. Not here, honey. On page 64, the small skillet is the whole trick. Melt 1 teaspoon of butter in the 8 inch skillet on medium until it foams.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b010_.text: Pour the beaten eggs in. As the edge is set, push them to the middle and tip the pan so the raw egg runs out. When the top is almost set, put the cheese and chopped ham on half, fold it over, and slide it onto one plate. It cooks in three minutes, and it uses up every bit of cheese and ham left in your fridge. Two eggs, one little pan, and one plate. Now let me tell you about Harold. Harold ate two eggs every morning, and after he passed, I quit eating breakfast. Then I made two eggs in my little pan and said, Two eggs, his way, in my little pan. That's what brought me back to the table. The eggs keep going, and the heels wait at number 20. Number 11 is Slow Scrambled Eggs, page 65. Most homes crank the burner up high, and the eggs go tough and dry before the toast is even done. The low heat is the whole secret.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b011_.text: Stir slowly, pulling the eggs in from the edges, and they come out soft and creamy, the way the hotel in Des Moines used to serve them. Salt goes in at the end. Salt at the beginning makes them weep water. Cook them until there's no runny part left. Eggs that bake in a little dish come next, and they sound much fancier than they are. Number 12 is Sheared Eggs in a Ramekin, page 67. Most folks hover at the stove, hoping the yolks don't break. Mine go in a little dish instead. It sounds fancy, and it's the easiest supper in my book. Put the cream in the bottom, crack two eggs on top, and sprinkle the cheese and some pepper. It's pennies a plate, honey. Eat it right from the dish with toast for dipping. Slip chopped ham or spinach under the eggs for a whole supper. Three eggs make two plates, tonight and tomorrow. Number 13, The Little Frittata, page 68.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b012_.text: Most folks dirty two dishes for eggs. Here it's one pan, the 8-inch skillet. Potato, onion, and oil go in until golden, about 5 minutes, then the ham, then the eggs, with cheese on top. 2 minutes on the stove, then 10 to 12 minutes in the oven, until the middle is set. Use a skillet with a metal handle. A plastic handle can't go in the oven. Cut it in half, and the second half is good cold with a pickle. Next, one muffin tin holds a whole week of egg breakfasts. Number 14, ham and cheese egg muffins for one week, page 70. Most folks crack eggs one at a time into a hot pan. Here's six eggs baked in a tin with ham, cheese, and onion, 40 cents each. Bake at 350 for 20 to 22 minutes until a knife comes out clean. Paper liners stick to eggs, so grease the tin well or use silicone cups.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b013_.text: Cool them, then keep them four days in the fridge or a month in the freezer. On a busy morning, 30 seconds in the microwave. Next, the old church breakfast. Eggs in white sauce over toast. Number 15 is creamed eggs on toast, page 71. Most folks picture a church basement crowd. Melt one tablespoon of butter in a small pot. Stir in one of flour and cook it one minute. Whisk in the milk slowly and stir until it's thick, about three minutes. Fold in two chopped hard-boiled eggs, spoon it over two slices of toast and dust with paprika. Add a spoon of chopped ham or dried beef to the sauce and it's a Sunday supper. Number 16, page 73, and this one you eat sitting down. Most folks eat standing up at the counter. Crack one egg in a small skillet and cook it two minutes. Turn it, lay a slice of cheese on top, and cook one more minute. That cheese needs help.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b014_.text: I put a lid on the pan for that last minute and it melts perfect. Toast two slices, butter them, and the whole plate costs pennies. Cook the yolk until it's firm, honey. Next, my mother's canning jar ring. Number 17, Egg and Cheese English Muffin, page 102. Loose in the pan, a fried egg hangs out over the muffin. So my mother's trick is a grease canning jar ring. The ring is the right size for an English muffin. Crack the egg inside it, break the yolk, and cover the pan two minutes. Then lift the ring, turn the egg, and add the cheese and ham on top for one minute. Set it in the muffin, honey. October apples come next in the little skillet. Number 18, fried apples, page 147. Most folks reach for a sugary box. I melt a teaspoon of butter in a small skillet and lay in one sliced apple. Turn them and cook five minutes.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b015_.text: Tart apples hold their shape and sweet ones turn to applesauce, which is good too. Sprinkle brown sugar and a pinch of cinnamon. Then cook three minutes more. It costs pennies and the kitchen smells like fall. Then a cup of leftover rice turns into something sweet. Number 19, rice pudding from leftover rice. Page 157. Most folks let leftover rice sit until it's hard as a doorstop. I put a cup of cooked rice in a small pot with milk and sugar and I stir it. It thickens as it cools, so I take it off while it still looks loose. Raisins and vanilla go in and I eat it warm or cold with cinnamon. Two small bowls and it costs pennies. Nothing gets wasted here, which brings us to the end of the loaf everybody throws away. Number 20, Bread Pudding from the Heels, page 159. Most of us toss the heels or give them to the birds.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b016_.text: I keep a bag of them in the freezer instead, and when there are four, I cube them into a small buttered dish. Beat one egg with three quarters of a cup of milk, two tablespoons of sugar, a drop of vanilla, a pinch of cinnamon, and a few raisins. Pour that over the bread, press it down, and wait ten minutes. Bake at 350 degrees for 30 minutes until puffed and set. It makes two bowls, a spoon of warm caramel on top, and it's dessert for company. Carry one bowl to the table and sit down. One person, one little dish, and not one crumb wasted, honey. Every one of these twenty came from my little book, Supper for One. Pull up a chair, honey. Every one of these twenty breakfasts is a page in my little cookbook. Supper for One is the title, and every recipe in it makes one or two portions. The link is in the description below.

D:\\wt\\lcfbrk\\vlog\\lcfbrk\\voz\\b017_.text: Holidays are coming, so let's talk mashed potatoes next. Thanksgiving is coming, so go watch most people make mashed potatoes wrong. Try these church lady tricks before Thanksgiving on my other channel. It's called Loretta's Church Kitchen. Then come right back, because I've got a small job for you tonight. Before you get up from this chair, set one place at the table for tomorrow's breakfast and eat it sitting down, not standing at the counter. Then tell me, which breakfast did your mother make on a cold morning that you still think about? Tell me the number too. I read every one. Leave that little skillet on the back burner because next week I'm cooking more small suppers for one and you're welcome at my table. Set the table, pour your coffee, and sit down like company is coming. Use the good plate. You're worth it. Bye now and God bless. I'll see you next week.
